text: Twelve hours. You've been locked in a room with hot pizza, a brand-new game console and six puppies, live on national TV.|And you haven't looked up from your book once.
Is he even human?!
Three months ago, you couldn't get out of bed before noon. Forty-seven projects started. Zero finished.
So what happened? What if you gained unlimited discipline?
Meet you, before all this. Seventeen years old. Screen time: nine hours and forty-one minutes a day.
A guitar you played twice. A gym membership you used once. A science project due tomorrow that you haven't started, because there's always later.
Everyone has a little voice that says later. Five more minutes. Tomorrow. Next Monday. Yours was the loudest voice in the house.
Max! It's two in the afternoon!
Then, at three in the morning, scrolling in the dark, an app you never downloaded asks you one question.
Remove the voice that says later? You press accept. Obviously. You weren't really reading.
In the morning, the voice is gone. Completely silent.
Day one. Four fifty-nine in the morning. Your alarm is set for five. You turn it off before it rings.|No snooze, no fight, no drama. Your body just goes.
Push-up number one hundred. Your room, which hasn't been clean since you were twelve, is clean in four minutes.
Mom! Max is being weird!
Cold shower? Fine. Broccoli for breakfast? Fine. Your phone goes into a drawer, and you don't even miss it.
Why are you eating a tree?
At school you do something nobody has ever seen. You finish the science project in the first break. Then you start next week's.
Bro. Are you sick? Blink twice if you need help.
Here's the strange part. You don't feel motivated. You don't feel anything special.|You decide to do a thing, and you do it. No gap.
Day four. You walk into the gym, and you can't lift the empty bar.
Look who's here! Noodle arms! See you never, buddy.
Tyler has said that to every new guy for three years. And he's usually right. Most people quit in the first month.
But you come back the next day. And the next. Same time, every day. Rain or snow, tired or not.
Scientists in London found that a new habit takes about sixty-six days to become automatic. You don't need sixty-six days. You need zero.
Day ten, you run one kilometer and almost die. Day twenty, five kilometers. Day thirty, ten.
Day forty. One thousand push-ups before breakfast. The neighbors think you're building something, because they hear counting through the wall.
You practice guitar three hours a day. Your fingertips hurt. You put tape on them and keep going.
Spanish on the bus. Chess at lunch. Coding at night. And exactly eight hours of sleep, because sleep is on the schedule too.
Max... did you clean the whole kitchen?
You cleaned the whole house. And the garage. And the neighbor's garage.
Your screen time drops to eleven minutes a day. Your grades go from D's to straight A's.
Day sixty-six. The school talent show. The kid who never finished anything walks on stage with a guitar.
Five minutes before your turn, you open the guitar case. Five of the six strings are cut. Somebody really doesn't want you up there.
You don't panic. Panic is just a feeling, and feelings don't make your decisions anymore. You play the whole song on one string.
Three minutes later, the whole hall is on its feet. Someone films it. By the morning, it has two million views.
And at the gym, Tyler watches you load one hundred kilograms on the bar.
No way. No way!
You lift it. Five times. Then you go back to your schedule, because there's still one set left.
Day eighty. Something about you has changed, and it's not just the muscles. People have a word for it. Aura.
When you walk down the hallway, people step aside. Teachers stand up straighter. The principal calls you sir. By accident.
Half the school starts copying you. Five a.m. alarms. Broccoli at lunch. Most of them quit by Wednesday.
The other half starts to hate you. Because when one person suddenly has no excuses, everyone else's excuses start to look very small.
Nobody is that perfect. He's faking it. And I'm going to prove it.
Rumors spread. He takes pills. He's a robot. His mom does his homework. Even Jay starts to look at you differently.
You don't really have time for me anymore, huh?
And Tyler finds the perfect way to expose you. On live TV.
Day one hundred. The talent show video reaches a TV station, and they make a whole show about one question: can anyone tempt Max?
The man who designed every trap in that room is Tyler.
Pizza! Puppies! Come on, man, just look at them! One look!
So they lock you in that room. The pizza gets cold. The console plays its own music.|One puppy falls asleep on your shoe. You turn the page.
Twelve hours! He's still reading the same book! Somebody check if he's alive!
You finish the book. Then the next one. You read a book a day now. Three hundred and sixty-five a year.
Scientists ask to scan your brain. The part that usually argues with you about every hard thing? Quiet. Like a library at midnight.
You learn to solve a Rubik's cube blindfolded. Then you learn seven languages, so you can say no to dessert in all of them.
Day one hundred and fifty. You notice something. Almost nobody is truly disciplined, so almost nobody can keep up with you.
You code an app at night. It's called Now. It has one button, and it deletes every excuse from your to-do list.
Ten thousand downloads. Then one million. Then ten million. Your garage turns into an office with twelve workers, all older than you.|One of them is your mom.
So you're rich now?
Not rich. But your bank account has more zeros than your old report card.
Then the biggest tech company in the world calls. They want to buy your app for one hundred million dollars.|The meeting is on Friday, at seven in the evening.
But something is wrong, and you're the last one to notice.
The voice that said later was also the voice that said rest. Stop. That's enough for today. And that voice is gone too.
Your knee starts hurting on a run. You finish twenty kilometers anyway. Then you limp for two weeks, and you train on crutches.
Jay's birthday party? Not on the schedule. Movie night? Not productive. And your little sister?
Max, will you play with me?
You set a timer. Fifteen minutes. When it rings, you stand up in the middle of her story and walk out.
Oh. Okay.
You have perfect discipline. And you are slowly turning into a machine.
Friday. Six forty-five. You're standing in a suit outside a glass tower. One hundred million dollars is fifteen minutes away.
Your phone buzzes. A video from Mom. Mia, on the school stage, in a paper star costume, looking at the door. Looking for you.
You forgot. You promised her two months ago. Her first solo. At seven.
Everything in you says: follow the plan. That's what discipline is. That's who you are now.
And for the first time since the voice disappeared, you do the hardest thing a perfectly disciplined person can do. You stop.
Then you run. Not in sneakers. In dress shoes. Two kilometers. Your knee is screaming. You don't care.
Six fifty-nine. You burst through the doors of the school hall. Mia sees you.|And she sings the best song a seven-year-old has ever sung.
You came! You really came!
You lose the deal. The company buys another shop the next morning.
And somehow, that's fine. Because now you understand. Discipline is a tool, not a boss.|It should carry you toward the people you love, not away from them.
So you change the schedule. Monday: Mia, two hours, no timer. Wednesday: Jay. Sunday: absolutely nothing. You do nothing with perfect discipline.
Wait. You're actually coming to my party?
You show up early. Obviously.
One year later. You run your first marathon on a healed knee, and Mia holds the sign at the finish line.
Your app has fifty million users. Your guitar gets new strings every month. And Tyler? He asks if you'll be his gym partner.
Teach me, man. Please.
Then, at three in the morning, your phone lights up. The same app. A new update. Unlimited courage. Accept?
Your thumb is right above the button.
If you had unlimited discipline, what's the first thing you would do? Tell me in the comments.|And subscribe, so you don't miss what happens when Max presses accept.
